rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six compounds and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The midpoint temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Injection 1 already achieved the maximum CRF, with substantial resolution margin. Shorten the gradient while holding the solvent window and temperature fixed to test a faster method and measure the critical pairs' sensitivity to gradient slope.

Both runs achieved maximum CRF, and the 8-minute gradient retains ample resolution. Test a 4-minute gradient to approach the shortest fully resolved method while measuring whether the early critical pair remains above R = 1.5.

The 4-minute gradient achieves maximum CRF but leaves little resolution margin for the first pair. Test higher temperature at the same slope to shorten retention and determine whether temperature improves or erodes that pair's selectivity.

Heating reduced selectivity for the critical early pair, so test the low-temperature limit at the same gradient slope. Improved resolution could provide enough margin to shorten the gradient further or raise its starting organic fraction.

Cooling improved the critical pair's resolution from 1.65 to 2.48. Test the minimum gradient duration at this favorable temperature to establish whether full resolution survives the faster separation.

Narrowing the gradient window reduces its slope enough to potentially raise the critical pair from R = 1.23 to above 1.5 while retaining the minimum gradient duration. The last compound will likely elute during the final hold, so this run tests the trade-off between early-pair resolution and late retention.

Shift the successful 0.70-wide gradient window upward, preserving its slope while restoring strong final elution to accelerate the last compound. This tests whether the early pair retains sufficient resolution at a higher starting organic fraction.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten late retention while making the gradient slightly shallower. Monitor the first pair closely, since its earlier elution could offset the resolution benefit of the reduced slope.

Use the improved early-pair resolution margin to test a 5 C temperature increase, which should shorten the last peak's retention. Keep the gradient unchanged to determine whether full resolution survives this modest heating step.

Test one higher starting organic fraction to shorten the separation and reduce gradient steepness. This probes the upper starting-solvent boundary: the first peak is already near the dead-time region, so early-pair compression may become limiting.

Return to the successful starting fraction and slightly flatten the gradient to offset the selectivity loss expected from another 5 C temperature increase. This tests whether warmer operation can preserve full resolution without materially extending late-peak retention.

Test whether cooling restores full resolution at the higher starting organic fraction that failed at 30 C. This completes the local temperature–starting-solvent comparison while retaining the fastest gradient and strongest final elution.

The higher starting fraction compresses the early pair even at 25 C, so return to 0.25 and slightly reduce the final fraction to improve resolution margin. This targets a maximum-CRF, 2-minute gradient with better early retention than the fastest fully resolved method so far.

Raise temperature one step from injection 14 to shorten late retention while testing whether its early-pair resolution margin remains sufficient. The lower starting fraction avoids the near-dead-time compression seen at phi0 = 0.35.

Test one temperature step above injection 10, the fastest fully resolved method so far, while preserving strong final elution. This directly checks the temperature boundary for further shortening; injection 10 remains the fallback if the early pair falls below R = 1.5.

Back off to the successful 30 C temperature and slightly flatten the gradient to seek additional resolution margin around injection 10. This should retain a short, maximum-CRF separation while testing a neighboring final-solvent setting.

Cooling this neighboring method should improve the limiting early pair while keeping all six peaks well within the unpenalized time window. Maximum CRF is already secured; this tests a short alternative with greater resolution margin.

Shift the successful 0.65-wide window downward to retain the early peaks farther from the dead-time region while preserving gradient slope. This tests another maximum-CRF candidate, with some expected delay of the last peak during the final hold.

Raise the starting fraction one step from injection 19 to shorten retention and flatten the gradient, aiming to improve the limiting early-pair resolution. This refines the short, fully resolved region while keeping the first peak away from the near-unretained conditions seen at phi0 = 0.35.

Raise temperature one step to shorten the final-hold retention of injection 20 while using its early-pair resolution margin. This targets another maximum-CRF method; injection 10 remains the fastest fully resolved method observed.

Raise the starting fraction one step from injection 21 to shorten retention while slightly reducing gradient steepness. Nearby runs suggest this starting fraction can preserve full resolution at 30 C, whereas 0.35 causes early-pair compression.

Cool the latest fully resolved method to increase the critical pair's resolution margin while retaining the minimum gradient duration. Maximum CRF is already achieved; this tests a nearby alternative with greater separation margin, while injection 10 remains the fastest fully resolved option.

Increase the final organic fraction from injection 19 to accelerate the last peak while preserving stronger early retention than the phi0 = 0.30 methods. The same gradient width gave full resolution in injection 8, making this a promising short, maximum-CRF alternative.

Raise the final organic fraction one step from injection 24 to shorten late retention; slope scaling predicts the critical pair will remain near R = 1.5. Maximum CRF is already secured, and injection 10 remains the fastest fully resolved method observed.
